tool_arguments.query: NVIDIA Data Center revenue Q4 fiscal 2026 growth drivers

events.content: NVIDIA Data Center revenue Q4 fiscal 2026 growth drivers

NVIDIA’s Data Center revenue was **$62.314 billion in Q4 FY2026** (quarter ended January 25, 2026), versus **$35.580 billion in Q4 FY2025**—an increase of **$26.734 billion, or 75% year over year**. [[1]]

**Primary growth drivers**

- **Blackwell system demand and the Blackwell Ultra ramp:** Management said the 75% year-over-year increase was driven primarily by sustained Blackwell strength and the ramp of Blackwell Ultra; Grace Blackwell systems represented roughly two-thirds of quarterly Data Center revenue. [[2]]
- **AI training and inference infrastructure build-out:** NVIDIA attributed Data Center growth to the structural shifts toward accelerated computing and AI, with rising inference deployments in addition to training workloads. [[3]] [[2]]
- **Broad-based customer demand:** Cloud providers, hyperscalers, AI-model developers, enterprises, and sovereign customers all contributed, while hyperscalers remained more than 50% of Data Center revenue and growth was led by the remainder of the customer base as revenue diversified. [[2]] [[1]]
- **Networking was the fastest-growing component:** Networking revenue reached **$10.980 billion**, up **263% year over year**, versus Data Center compute revenue of **$51.334 billion**, up **58%**. [[1]]
- **NVLink, Ethernet, and InfiniBand adoption:** The networking surge reflected the introduction and continuing ramp of NVLink compute fabric for GB200 and GB300 systems, plus growth in Spectrum-X Ethernet and InfiniBand; management specifically identified NVLink 72 scale-up switches as the principal year-over-year networking driver. [[1]] [[2]]
- **Demand extended to prior architectures:** NVIDIA said Hopper and even much of its older Ampere-based cloud product inventory were sold out, illustrating that demand exceeded just the Blackwell transition. [[2]] 

In short, Q4 FY2026 Data Center growth was chiefly a **Blackwell/Grace Blackwell rack-scale AI-computing ramp**, amplified by an exceptionally strong **networking attach** and broader AI infrastructure spending across cloud and non-cloud customers. [[2]] [[1]]

tool_arguments.query: NVIDIA Data Center segment definition fiscal 2026

events.content: NVIDIA Data Center segment definition fiscal 2026

NVIDIA defines **Data Center** as a market platform—not one of its reportable operating segments; its two operating segments are **Compute & Networking** and **Graphics**. [[1]] 

In fiscal 2026, the Data Center platform targeted compute-intensive AI, data processing, graphics, robotics, and scientific-computing workloads across cloud, hyperscale, on-premises, and edge data centers. [[2]] It comprised data-center compute and networking infrastructure—typically supplied as rack-scale systems, subsystems, or modules—plus software and services. [[2]] 

Its networking scope includes NVLink interconnects and switches; InfiniBand and Ethernet platforms; network adapters, cables, DPUs, switch chips and systems; and related software. [[2]]

tool_arguments.query: NVIDIA Data Center revenue growth drivers Q2 fiscal 2027 Blackwell Ultra networking

events.content: NVIDIA Data Center revenue growth drivers Q2 fiscal 2027 Blackwell Ultra networking

**Q2 FY2027 Data Center performance.** NVIDIA generated **$89.0 billion** of Data Center revenue in the quarter ended July 26, 2026—up **18% sequentially** from $75.2 billion in Q1 FY2027, or about **$13.8 billion** of incremental revenue, and up **117% year over year**. [[1, 2]]

**Principal growth driver: Blackwell-based AI compute deployment.** Sustained Blackwell demand drove hyperscaler revenue to **$49 billion**, up **13% sequentially**, as customers added GPU capacity; management characterized the dynamic as additional compute capacity translating directly into additional customer revenue. [[3]]

**Broader customer mix was also important.** Data Center growth came from both hyperscalers and the AI-cloud, industrial and enterprise (“ACIE”) customer group; ACIE revenue was roughly **$40 billion**, rising **25% quarter over quarter** and **138% year over year**, aided by NeoCloud partners bringing capacity online. [[4]]

**Blackwell Ultra increased content per AI factory.** GB300 and other Blackwell Ultra systems are optimized for agentic, reasoning and physical AI, while NVIDIA’s Blackwell architecture combines 36 Grace CPUs and 72 Blackwell GPUs in a data-center-scale liquid-cooled design. [[5]] NVIDIA placed the Grace Blackwell revenue opportunity at approximately **$25 billion per gigawatt**, versus roughly **$18 billion per gigawatt** for Hopper, indicating that the platform transition raises NVIDIA content per unit of deployed power capacity. [[3]]

**Networking was a material complementary engine.** Networking had another record quarter, with revenue up **18% sequentially**; Spectrum-X Ethernet grew **2.6x year over year**, demonstrating that AI-cluster buildouts require substantial scale-out networking alongside GPU compute. [[3]] The prior-year platform ramp context supports this: NVIDIA said Data Center networking revenue had grown **142%** in FY2026, driven by NVLink compute fabric for GB200/GB300 systems and continued Ethernet and InfiniBand growth. [[5]]

**Bottom line.** Q2’s Data Center acceleration reflected a mutually reinforcing stack: Blackwell/Blackwell Ultra compute capacity, higher system-level content per gigawatt, expansion beyond a small set of hyperscalers into AI clouds and enterprises, and rapidly growing NVLink, InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. [[3, 4]]
